# Glossary {.unnumbered}

[Climate scenarios]{.glossary-term #gloss-climate-scenarios}
: Six warming pathways used in Q-CRAFT, based on IPCC Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). The coolest is Paris-aligned (below 2°C warming by 2100, SSP1-2.6). The hottest is Hot + Unadapted (high warming with slow adaptation, SSP3-7.0 at the 90th percentile). Climate impacts on GDP are derived from the FADCP Climate Dataset [(Centorrino, Massetti, and Tagklis, 2024)](references.qmd#src-centorrino-2024), building on the empirical estimates of [Kahn et al. (2021)](references.qmd#src-kahn-2021). See the IMF User Guide, Section IV.B for detailed methodology.

[C-PIMA (Climate Public Investment Management Assessment)]{.glossary-term #gloss-c-pima}
: An IMF framework for evaluating how well a country's public investment management institutions account for climate change. C-PIMA engagements can include Q-CRAFT modelling of the fiscal impacts of climate scenarios for the assessed country. Uganda's 2024 assessment reports one such analysis. See the C-PIMA Handbook [(IMF, 2025)](references.qmd#src-imf-2025-cpima) for the full framework.

[DSA (Debt Sustainability Analysis)]{.glossary-term #gloss-dsa}
: A framework used by the IMF and World Bank to assess whether a country's debt is sustainable (whether the government can meet its current and future debt obligations without debt relief or arrears). Q-CRAFT can complement a DSA with long-term climate-adjusted fiscal trajectories.

[Debt dynamics equation]{.glossary-term #gloss-debt-dynamics-equation}
: The core equation in Q-CRAFT: $d_t = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + r_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t$. Next year's debt-to-GDP ratio equals the current ratio, adjusted for the interest-growth differential, minus the primary balance. When interest rates exceed growth ($r > g$), debt rises automatically: the government must run a primary surplus even to hold debt still. See the IMF User Guide, Section IV.A on debt dynamics for detailed derivation and corollaries.

[Debt-to-GDP ratio]{.glossary-term #gloss-debt-to-gdp-ratio}
: Total government debt expressed as a percentage of nominal GDP. The standard measure of a country's debt burden, since it scales debt relative to the economy's ability to service it. Q-CRAFT projects this ratio through 2099 under baseline and climate scenarios.

[Expenditure rigidity]{.glossary-term #gloss-expenditure-rigidity}
: The degree to which government spending resists downward adjustment when climate shocks reduce GDP. Measured on a 0-1 scale. A value of 1.0 means spending is fully sticky: it stays at the baseline level in local currency terms even as GDP falls, the worst case for debt accumulation. A value of 0.0 means spending adjusts fully with GDP, maintaining the baseline expenditure-to-GDP ratio. This parameter only affects climate scenarios, not the baseline. See the IMF User Guide, pp. 20 and 35-36.

[Fiscal rule]{.glossary-term #gloss-fiscal-rule}
: A mechanism in Q-CRAFT that adjusts primary expenditure to steer debt toward a target ratio. When enabled, the model computes the debt-stabilizing primary balance and adjusts spending by the fiscal gap (the difference between the actual and debt-stabilizing primary balance). The adjustment is additive in levels (not a rate) and depends on the prior year's state, so the model must compute it year by year. See the IMF User Guide, pp. 15-18.

[DIGNAD (Debt, Investment, Growth, and Natural Disasters)]{.glossary-term #gloss-dignad}
: An IMF dynamic general equilibrium model of natural disasters and public investment in developing countries. As a general equilibrium model it carries far more structure than Q-CRAFT's single recursion. Discussed in the co-design appendix as a tool that could benefit from the SovTech approach.

[Golden master]{.glossary-term #gloss-golden-master}
: In software verification, a reference output used to detect unintended changes. Q-CRAFT's golden master tests compare the Python engine's outputs against values extracted from the IMF's Excel workbook for the same country and parameter inputs. Parity with the Excel tool (not any independent calculation) is the acceptance criterion.

[LIC-DSF (Low-Income Country Debt Sustainability Framework)]{.glossary-term #gloss-lic-dsf}
: The IMF-World Bank framework for assessing debt sustainability in low-income countries, built around country-specific debt burden thresholds. Compared against Q-CRAFT in Module 5, and discussed in the co-design appendix as a more complex tool that could benefit from the SovTech approach.

[Interest-growth differential]{.glossary-term #gloss-interest-growth-differential}
: The difference between the nominal interest rate on government debt ($r$) and nominal GDP growth ($g$), expressed as $(r - g) / (1 + g)$. When positive ($r > g$), debt dynamics are unfavorable: the debt ratio rises automatically. When negative ($g > r$), debt dynamics are favorable. This single variable determines whether debt is self-stabilizing or self-reinforcing.

[Primary balance]{.glossary-term #gloss-primary-balance}
: Government revenue minus non-interest expenditure (primary expenditure), expressed as a share of GDP. The primary balance is the fiscal variable a government can control in the near to medium term. A primary surplus means the government generates enough revenue to cover its non-interest spending. A primary deficit means it does not.

[WEO (World Economic Outlook)]{.glossary-term #gloss-weo}
: The IMF's flagship publication providing analysis and projections of the global economy. Q-CRAFT uses the WEO database as the source for macroeconomic and fiscal data through the medium-term forecast horizon: the Explorer's Verified mode runs the October 2024 release the workbook ships, and Current mode, the default, runs April 2026, with the horizon marked on every chart. A country's projection starts from the last year that carries the data the model needs, which for a few countries is earlier than the release boundary. The Explorer names that anchor year on screen wherever it differs from the release boundary. Beyond the anchor year, Q-CRAFT's own projection methodology takes over.

[SovTech]{.glossary-term #gloss-sovtech}
: The application of SupTech (supervisory technology) principles (modularity, open source, human-centered design) to sovereign debt analysis and public financial management tools. Q-CRAFT Explorer is a proof of concept for this approach.
